slides.title: Seoul: The Carrot and the Stick
slides.inOneSentence: The title slide, where you introduce yourself, ask the class about composting, and promise five ideas New York could borrow from Seoul.
background: The title comes from an old saying about getting a donkey to move. You can hold a carrot in front of it as a reward, or tap it with a stick as a punishment. In city climate policy, a carrot is something like a cheap loan, a subsidy or reward points. A stick is something like a fine or a ban. The talk looks at how Seoul and New York use these two kinds of tools on the same problem, which is getting existing buildings to pollute less.

Seoul is a fair match for New York. The city of Seoul has about 9.4 million people and New York City about 8.3 million. Both cities are very dense and build tall, and in both, buildings cause roughly two-thirds of the greenhouse gas emissions. Neither city has empty land left for big new parks. Because they face the same limits, an idea that works in Seoul has a real chance of working in New York.

You open with composting because everyone can picture it. Seoul uses shared smart bins for food waste. A resident taps a card, the bin weighs what goes in, and that household is billed by weight. New York made curbside composting mandatory, but in 2025 organics were only about 2.4% of the residential waste the city collected. Most people in the room probably did not compost last night, so the question opens the comparison in a friendly way.

You also tell the class early that one Seoul policy is in trouble right now. Since January 1, 2026, Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi can no longer send household trash straight to a landfill. The region did not build enough incinerators in time, so some trash is now sent to other regions. Slide 15 covers this. Saying it on the first slide shows the class you will include Seoul's problems along with its successes.

The five ideas come on slide 19: food waste charged by weight, city loans for building retrofits, balcony solar kits, a transit pass named for the climate, and removing a highway the way Seoul did at Cheonggyecheon. You only need to promise them here.

questions.q: Why compare New York with Seoul? Why not a city in Europe?
questions.a: Seoul matches New York on the hard parts. The city populations are close (about 9.4 million and 8.3 million), both cities are dense and tall, and buildings cause roughly two-thirds of emissions in both. Neither has open land for big new parks, so lessons move between them more easily.

questions.q: What exactly is the carrot and what is the stick?
questions.a: For existing buildings, Seoul's main tool is a carrot. Its Building Retrofit Program lent owners cheap city money for upgrades, and from 2013 it lent up to 100% of the eligible cost at 1.75% interest. New York's main tool is a stick. Local Law 97 fines owners $268 for every ton of CO₂e their building emits over its limit.

questions.q: Doesn't Seoul use sticks too?
questions.a: Yes. Korea has made people buy priced trash bags since 1995, and Seoul's smart bins bill food waste by weight. Under Korea's national rules, many new buildings must meet a zero-energy grade. The most polluting diesel vehicles (Grade 5) are banned from central Seoul, and the 2026 landfill ban is a rule with no reward attached. The title describes the main tool each city uses on buildings that already exist. For those, Seoul leans on loans and rewards and New York leans on fines.

questions.q: Is composting actually required in New York?
questions.a: Yes, curbside composting is mandatory. In 2025, organics were only about 2.4% of residential waste collected, up from 1.4% in 2024. Fines were set to start in April 2025, were paused within three weeks, and came back on January 1, 2026, with 330 summonses in the first stretch.

questions.q: Which Seoul policy is struggling?
questions.a: The ban on sending household trash straight to landfills, which started January 1, 2026. It was passed in 2021 with five years to prepare, but the region did not add enough incinerators. Seoul has only four, and most are 20 to 30 or more years old, so some districts now send trash to other regions. Slide 15 covers it.

dontSay: Don't present Seoul as a perfect model. You bring up the 2026 waste crisis on purpose.
Don't say Seoul only uses carrots. It also uses priced trash bags, fines, vehicle bans and Korea's national zero-energy rules for new buildings.

Don't give a number for how many Seoul households use the weighing bins. Your sources don't have one.

slides.title: Comparing the Two Cities
slides.inOneSentence: Seoul and New York side by side on population, the share of emissions that comes from buildings, and the main policy each city uses on existing buildings.
background: The two cities are close in size. Seoul has about 9.4 million people in the city and about 26 million in the metro area. New York has about 8.3 million in the city and about 20 million in the metro area. All four numbers are rounded. Both cities are very dense and build tall, and both rely heavily on transit (New York's use is very high by US standards). Seoul's housing is mostly apartments, and New York has a mix of building types. Neither city has free land for big new parks.

Buildings are the biggest source of emissions in both cities. Seoul's current climate plan puts buildings at 67% of the city's greenhouse gas emissions. New York's share changes from one emissions inventory to the next, between 66 and 71%, so the slide shows a range. In both cities, about two-thirds of the problem comes from the buildings themselves.

Seoul's main tool for older buildings is the Building Retrofit Program (BRP), which started in 2008. Under it, the city lent owners money to upgrade their buildings so they would use less energy. It was extended to private buildings such as universities and hospitals, then to homes in 2012, when it grew under One Less Nuclear Power Plant. In 2013 Seoul cut the interest rate from 2.5% to 1.75% a year and raised the most it would lend from 80% to 100% of the eligible cost. After that, an owner could borrow up to the full eligible cost from the city at a low rate and pay it back over time. Your sources don't say whether these exact terms still apply. Seoul's current climate plan talks about long-term interest-free loans for upgrades to existing buildings.

New York's main tool is Local Law 97 (LL97), passed in 2019. It covers buildings over 25,000 square feet. Each building gets a yearly carbon limit per square foot based on how it is used, for example offices or apartments. If a building goes over its limit, the owner pays $268 for every ton of CO₂e above it. The law aims for 40% lower emissions by 2030 and 80% lower by 2050, compared with 2005. The limits get much stricter in 2030. About 11% of covered buildings were estimated to be over the 2024 to 2029 limits, and about 63% are projected to be over the 2030 limits if nothing changes.

Put together, this is where the title comes from. Seoul helps owners pay for upgrades, and New York charges owners who stay over the limit. Your sources describe LL97 as leaving the financing to owners. That gap is the reason for your main recommendation on slide 19, a city loan program for retrofits that works alongside LL97.

slides.inOneSentence: Where Seoul's greenhouse gas emissions come from, with buildings at about two-thirds, plus the 2005 total that all of Seoul's targets are measured against.
background: The donut chart splits Seoul's emissions into three parts. Buildings are 67%, transportation is 18%, and other sectors make up the last 15%. The climate plan gives buildings at 67% and buildings plus transportation together at 85%, so transportation works out to 85 minus 67, or 18%. Your sources don't break down the other 15%, so the legend just says "Other sectors."

Sources give slightly different numbers for buildings. The current plan says 67%, Seoul's 2020 Green New Deal release said 68.2%, and a UNESCAP paper using 2018 data said 68.8%. They all land close to two-thirds, which is why you say "roughly two-thirds" out loud. Your sources also disagree on which year the 67% describes, so don't name one. Separately, buildings use 56% of all the energy Seoul consumes. That number measures energy use, so keep it apart from the emissions share.

Most of these emissions come from buildings that are already standing. Rules for new construction help, but they don't change the buildings people already live and work in. To cut most of its emissions, a city has to upgrade the buildings it already has. That is the job of Seoul's retrofit loans and of New York's LL97.

52.34 Mt CO₂e is Seoul's total emissions in 2005. Mt means million metric tons, and CO₂e means all greenhouse gases counted together as if they were CO₂. Seoul measures its 2033 target against 2005, which is called the baseline year. The plan aims to cut emissions to half of the 2005 level by 2033 and reach carbon neutrality (net zero) by 2050. slides.title: Seoul's Two Emergencies
slides.inOneSentence: The history behind Seoul's green policies, told through two crises, the Nanjido garbage dump and the 2011 energy scare after Fukushima and a Seoul blackout.
background: Seoul's green policies grew out of real problems. The timeline shows two of them. The first was a giant garbage dump on Nanjido, and the second was the energy scare of 2011.

Nanjido was an island in the Han River. In January 1977 work began on an embankment that joined it to the mainland, and in 1978 it became Seoul's official dump. The city chose it because it was easy to reach and far from downtown. Trash piled up in two mounds about 90 m high. At the time Korea had no modern way to treat landfill gas or leachate (the dirty liquid that drains out of trash), so the site leaked methane and toxic gases.

In 1993 the city decided to close the dump and start making the ground stable. Some sources say dumping ended in 1992. Planning for a park ran from 1991 to 1996, and building it took from 1996 to 2002. It opened as World Cup Park for the 2002 FIFA World Cup. Today the gas from the old trash is captured and used, the mounds are Haneul (Sky) Park and Noeul Park, and the site also holds the Seoul Energy Dream Center (slide 10). Slide 14 goes deeper into the park.

The second emergency came in 2011. The Fukushima nuclear accident happened in Japan, and the same year Seoul had a blackout. Seoul launched One Less Nuclear Power Plant as a direct response to these two events. Its first goal was to save or produce 2 million TOE of energy, about what one nuclear reactor produces in a year, through efficiency, energy saving and new renewables. Slide 6 covers the program.

Behind both stories is a basic fact about Korea. The country makes only about a fifth of its own energy (22.1% in 2024), which ranks it 35th of the 38 countries in the OECD. Your dossier calls this the pressure behind everything Seoul does on energy.

slides.explainSimply: Think of a family whose garage fills up with so much junk that it starts to smell. They seal it under a thick floor and build a nice room on top. Then, in 2011, the power goes out, and they push much harder on saving power. Seoul's story is like that. Its dump grew into two hills about 90 m high, roughly a 30-story building, and leaked gas. The city later closed it, captured the gas and built a park on top of the trash. Then in 2011 came Fukushima and a blackout in Seoul, and the city started One Less Nuclear Power Plant. Each problem pushed the city to act.

questions.q: Why did Seoul put its dump on an island in the river?
questions.a: Nanjido was easy to reach and far from downtown, which is why it was chosen in 1978. Work had started in 1977 on an embankment that joined the island to the mainland. Back then Korea had no modern system to treat landfill gas or the liquid draining out of the trash.

questions.q: When exactly did the dump close?
questions.a: The most cited version is that it was used from 1978 to 1993, when the city decided to close it and start making the ground stable. Some sources say dumping ended in 1992. The park opened in 2002.

questions.q: What did a blackout have to do with nuclear power?
questions.a: My sources say Seoul launched One Less Nuclear Power Plant in direct response to Fukushima and the 2011 Seoul blackout. The idea was to save or produce as much energy as one nuclear reactor makes, about 2 million TOE, through efficiency and new renewables. I don't have details on what caused the blackout, so I keep it to the year.

questions.q: Did Seoul actually shut down a nuclear plant?
questions.a: Not that my sources show. The name refers to the goal of saving or producing as much energy as one reactor makes. My sources describe it as a program about cutting demand and getting citizens to take part, and none of them say a reactor closed because of it. Phase 1 reached its 2 million TOE goal in June 2014, six months early.

questions.q: If Korea only makes 22.1% of its own energy, can one city's program really matter?
questions.a: It's one city, so I can't speak to the national effect. In Seoul, Phase 1 saved or produced 2.04 million TOE, and Eco-Mileage, the citizen rewards program, had 1.68 million participants by June 2014. Seoul's electricity self-sufficiency roughly doubled, from under 3% in 2011 to around 5% a few years later.

slides.title: Climate Targets and Car Bans
slides.inOneSentence: This slide shows Seoul's main climate plan: cut the city's emissions to half of the 2005 level by 2033, reach net zero by 2050, and push polluting vehicles out step by step.
background: Seoul's current climate plan is called the Basic Plan for Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth in Seoul. It is a 10-year plan. It starts from the amount of greenhouse gas the city gave off in 2005, which was 52.34 million tons of CO₂e. The 2033 target is measured against that 2005 number.

The plan has two big targets. The first is to cut emissions to half of the 2005 level by 2033. The second is to reach carbon neutrality, also called net zero, by 2050. Net zero means that whatever gas the city still gives off is balanced by gas taken back out of the air, so the total comes to zero. The bars between 2005, 2033 and 2050 follow a straight path only to make the picture easy to read. The plan sets the 2033 and 2050 targets and does not promise a straight path between them.
There is no recent total for Seoul's emissions in English sources, so you cannot say how far along the city is today. Stay with the 2005 starting point and the two targets.

Buildings cause about two-thirds of Seoul's emissions, and buildings and transport together cause 85%. So after buildings, transport is the next big piece. Korea rates vehicles from Grade 1 to Grade 5 by how much they pollute, and Grade 5 is the dirtiest. Grade 5 diesel vehicles are already banned citywide from December to March and all year in central Seoul. The plan then adds one step at a time: Grade 4 diesel vehicles out of central Seoul's green transport zones in 2025, Grade 4 vehicles banned citywide in 2030, all combustion engine vehicles banned from central Seoul in 2035, and banned citywide in 2050. On stage you say "gas and diesel cars," which is the plain way to say combustion engine vehicles. Your sources list 2025 as a plan date and don't confirm how that step was carried out, so call it the planned 2025 step.

The plan also aims for 279,000 electric vehicles by 2033, the same year as the halfway emissions target. The car bans are a useful reminder that Seoul uses firm rules as well as rewards. The next slides turn to the reward side, starting with energy.

slides.title: One Less Nuclear Power Plant
slides.inOneSentence: This slide explains Seoul's program to save or produce as much energy as one nuclear reactor makes in a year, and how it reached that goal six months early.
background: Two events in 2011 led to this program. The Fukushima nuclear disaster happened in Japan, and Seoul had a blackout the same year. In 2012 Seoul started a program called One Less Nuclear Power Plant. The idea was that the city could save or produce the same amount of energy that one nuclear reactor makes in a year. The program's name, One Less Nuclear Power Plant, comes from that idea.

The Phase 1 goal was 2 million TOE, which the city compared to the yearly output of one nuclear reactor. TOE means ton of oil equivalent. It is a unit that lets you add electricity, gas and other kinds of energy into one number. The plan split the goal into two parts: 1.59 million TOE from using less energy and 410,000 TOE from new renewable energy. Those are the 79% and 21% on the slide.

Seoul reached 2.04 million TOE in June 2014, six months early. The most effective single measure was Eco-Mileage, a voluntary rewards program for saving energy at home. It made each household's energy use something people could see and compare, and it gave small rewards for cutting it. By June 2014 it had 1.68 million participants, and together they saved 190,000 TOE. The 1.68 million comes back on the last slide. The 3D diagram labels its field of small homes "1.68 million households plus building retrofits." The label is a shorthand. The picture stands for the whole 2 million TOE goal, 1.59 million from saving energy and 410,000 from new renewables. The 1.68 million Eco-Mileage participants are only one part of it, the 190,000 TOE they saved. Say "participants" out loud, because that is what the sources count.

Phase 2 ran from 2014 to 2020 with bigger goals, including 20% of Seoul's electricity made inside the city. C40, a network of large cities working on climate, reports 4.65 million TOE of energy cut from 2012 to 2017. Electricity made in Seoul went from 2.9% in 2011 to about 5%. C40 says 5% and the city says 5.5% by 2015, so say it roughly doubled. About 5% is the latest figure in your sources, and it is far below the 20% goal. They give no final 2020 figure. The city set up the Seoul Energy Corporation to carry the work forward.

Korea makes little of its own energy. In 2024 it made 22.1%, 35th of 38 OECD countries. Seoul made under 3% of its own electricity in 2011. That low 2011 figure, along with Fukushima and the blackout the same year, helps explain why the city started by cutting how much energy it uses and asked residents to take part through programs like Eco-Mileage.

slides.title: Solar Panels on Balconies
slides.inOneSentence: This slide covers Solar City Seoul, a 2017 program that offered small solar kits for apartment balcony railings, with a goal of 1 GW more solar by 2022.
background: Solar City Seoul started in 2017. Its goals were 1 GW of new solar power by 2022 and solar for 1 million households. The budget was about ₩1.7 trillion, or about US$1.46 billion, and most of it was public money.

Seoul is a city of tall apartment blocks, so each apartment has very little roof. The city looked at balconies instead. It offered small standard solar kits that mount on the balcony railing. The kits were subsidized, renters could install them, and the city published design and safety standards for them. The target was 540,000 apartment balconies, plus 90,000 rental homes and 370,000 buildings. Those three parts add up to 1 million, the same as the household goal, though the dossier does not say that is how the goal was split.

By 2019 Seoul had 357.1 MW of solar across 285,000 households, and the program was described as ahead of its interim goal. 1 GW is 1,000 MW, so that is about a third of the way. A UN projection expected 583 MW by the end of 2020 and 1,015 MW by the end of 2022, but those were forecasts. Your sources do not give a final total for 2022.

The known barrier in Seoul was a lack of space on buildings and public facilities to put panels. Seoul also has a longer history of supporting small solar. In 2013 it became the first Korean city to pay small solar plants of 50 kW or less for each kWh they made, for five years.

For New York, the dossier calls balcony solar the idea New York could copy most directly. New York has hundreds of thousands of balconies, fire escapes and south-facing railings that make no power. The barriers are the building code, permits and landlord consent. New York would need a list of approved kits, a Department of Buildings process that doesn't require a full alteration filing for a plug-in kit, and a right for renters to install one. The dossier also points to Germany, where balcony solar spread quickly once permits got simpler.

slides.title: Paying for Building Retrofits
slides.inOneSentence: This slide puts Seoul's low-interest retrofit loans next to New York's Local Law 97 limits and fines, which is the main comparison of the whole talk.
background: Buildings use 56% of Seoul's energy and cause about two-thirds of its emissions. Most of those buildings are already standing, so the big question is how to pay for fixing them. A retrofit means upgrading an existing building, for example with insulation, better windows, new lighting or a new heating and cooling system.

Seoul's answer is the Building Retrofit Program, or BRP, which started in 2008. In 2012 it grew under One Less Nuclear Power Plant. It was opened to private buildings such as universities and hospitals, and in 2012 to homes. The city lends owners money at a low interest rate to pay for upgrades. In 2013 the city cut the rate from 2.5% to 1.75% a year and raised the most it would lend from 80% to 100% of the eligible cost, so an owner did not have to pay the eligible cost up front. The stated target is 90,000 buildings, which is 20% of Seoul's buildings that are over 20 years old.

Results depend on the source, so always name it. C40 reports 25,841 tons of CO₂ saved from 2012 to 2015 across about 4,200 projects, and other C40 reporting says 72,000 buildings were improved. A city report says 20,000 buildings and houses and 192,234 TOE of energy saved. A measured sample of 100 buildings (2012 to 2013) found that homes used 10% less energy and other buildings 6.5% less. Separately, 59 welfare facilities (social service buildings) were retrofitted and saved about 15% of their average energy use.

New York's answer is Local Law 97, passed in 2019. It covers buildings over 25,000 sq ft. Each building gets a yearly carbon limit per square foot, set by its type of use, such as offices or apartment buildings. The law does not tell owners what to fix. If a building goes over its limit, the owner pays $268 for each ton of CO₂e over the limit, every year. The overall goal is a 40% cut by 2030 and 80% by 2050, from 2005 levels.

The limits get much tighter in 2030. The office limit drops by 64.5% and the apartment building limit by 50.4% compared with 2024 to 2029. About 11% of covered buildings are estimated to be over the 2024 to 2029 limits, and about 63% are projected to be over the 2030 limits if nothing changes. LL97 leaves it to owners to find the money for upgrades. That gap is the reason for your second recommendation, a New York city loan for LL97 upgrades on terms like Seoul's.

slides.title: Zero-Energy Building Rules
slides.inOneSentence: Korea's national rules grade new buildings by how much of their own energy they make, and the rules started with public buildings in 2020 and reached private buildings in 2025.
background: Korea has a national system for zero-energy buildings, called ZEB for short. MOLIT, the national Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, sets the rules. Seoul's climate plan builds on this national system. So the rules on this slide apply across all of Korea, and Seoul's plan adds its own targets for new public buildings.

The system grades a building by its energy self-sufficiency rate. That is the share of the energy a building uses that it also makes itself, mostly with renewable systems such as solar panels. There are five grades. Grade 5 is the entry level, at 20 to 40%. Grade 1 is the top, at over 100%, which means the building makes more energy than it uses over a year. Your sources don't give confirmed percentages for Grades 4, 3 and 2. You only need to know that they sit between the two ends.

The rules came in steps, starting with the government's own buildings. In 2020, new public buildings over 1,000 m² had to meet ZEB status, and the size limit was later lowered to 500 m². In 2023, the public sector moved to Grade 5. The rule for private buildings was planned for 2024. It was pushed back one year after the construction industry objected, and talks with the industry ran into mid-2025. From 2025, private apartment complexes of 30 or more units and buildings over 1,000 m² in general have to meet Grade 5. Some sources also report a goal of making all new buildings in Korea zero-energy by 2030, but that date is less certain. Sources give slightly different dates for these steps, and you should say so on stage.
Seoul's climate plan sets its own targets for new public buildings: Grade 5 now, Grade 4 by 2030 and Grade 3 by 2050. So the plan raises the grade for new public buildings step by step over time.

This slide matters for the talk because it shows where the firm rules are. They come from Korea's national ZEB system, which Seoul's plan builds on, and they apply when a new building is designed and built. For buildings that already exist, Seoul leans on cheap loans (slide 8). New York's Local Law 97 covers large buildings over 25,000 sq ft, and most of those buildings already exist. It sets yearly carbon limits per square foot and fines owners who go over. The quote from MOLIT's Hong Seongjun explains why the private rule matters. Most buildings are private, so a rule for public buildings alone would reach only the smaller share of buildings.

questions.q: Why did Korea start with public buildings?

questions.q: How does this compare with New York's rules?

slides.title: Seoul Energy Dream Center
slides.inOneSentence: The Energy Dream Center, opened in 2012 on the old Nanjido landfill, is Korea's first zero-energy public building and covers its own yearly energy use.
background: The Seoul Energy Dream Center opened in 2012 in World Cup Park, in the Mapo-gu district. It is Korea's first zero-energy public building. It is about 3,500 m² and works as a public exhibition and education center about renewable energy. The Seoul city government commissioned it. The design was led by Fraunhofer ISE, a German research institute for solar energy, which ran a German and Korean team that designed the building and oversaw construction.

The site is the old Nanjido landfill from slide 4. Nanjido was an island in the Han River that became Seoul's official dump in 1978. Trash piled up about 90 m high in two mounds, and there was no modern system to treat the gas or the polluted liquid coming out of it. The city decided to close the dump in 1993, and the site reopened as World Cup Park for the 2002 World Cup. Landfill gas is now captured and used. Trash can't carry the weight of a building, so the Energy Dream Center stands on piles that go down through the waste to solid ground, with a reinforced concrete base plate on top. The dossier says only that the building sits on piles on a reinforced concrete base plate. Reaching solid ground is how piles usually work, and the dossier gives no depth for them.

The shape is the first energy strategy. The plan is square. The building widens as it rises over its three floors and turns 45°, with a square roof on top. From outside it looks a bit like a pinwheel with slanted walls, and it was shaped this way to cut how much energy the building needs. Wedge-shaped roof edges, called wings, stick out along the sides. They shade the windows, give cover at the entrance and hold solar panels. The white marble outside walls reflect sunlight, and one source says they reflect about 60% of it.

The envelope, meaning the walls, roof and windows, was designed to Passive House standards, so it is very well insulated and airtight. Geothermal heat pumps handle heating and cooling. Solar panels on the roof, on the wings and on a small patch of ground supply about 280,000 kWh a year, which covers the building's full yearly demand. The building stays connected to the power grid. It can send extra power out on sunny days and draw power when the panels make less than it needs. It is reported to use over 70% less energy than a similar ordinary building, and it holds Korea's KGBC green building certification and the Building Energy Efficiency Label.

The building connects the landfill story and the zero-energy story. It sits on the landfill Seoul turned into a park, and it shows the zero-energy idea from slide 9 working on a real public building in 2012, years before the national rule for public buildings began in 2020. New York has its own landfill that is becoming a park, Freshkills Park on Staten Island, so this is a place where the two cities line up closely.

slides.inOneSentence: Nowon Energy Zero House, finished in 2017 in Nowon-gu, is Korea's first zero-energy apartment complex, with 121 homes.
background: Nowon Energy Zero House, often called EZ House, is in Nowon-gu, a district of Seoul. It is Korea's first zero-energy apartment complex, with 121 apartments. It was finished in September 2017, and residents moved in from November 2017. Of all the Seoul buildings in the talk, this one matters most for New York, because New York has a huge number of apartment buildings and apartments are much harder to get to zero energy than a showcase building like the Energy Dream Center.

The goal is net zero over a year, counted in primary energy. That means the complex aims to make as much energy as it uses over a full year. The reported result is that it makes about 75 to 80% of its own energy, so say it aims for net zero and makes most of its own energy. Residents' energy costs are reported to be up to 61% lower than in similar ordinary apartments.

The dossier sums up the design as a passive envelope plus renewables. These are standard building parts, used together carefully. From the bottom up, the diagram shows a geothermal field with about 130 heat pumps, the structure, a Passive House envelope, heat recovery ventilation and, last, the solar panels. A Passive House envelope generally means thick insulation, an airtight layer and very good windows. Heat recovery ventilation brings in fresh air all the time and uses the stale air going out to warm or cool it, so little heat is lost. Heat recovery is shown on the diagram, but the dossier lists only a passive envelope plus renewables, so describe it in general terms if asked. Sources count the solar panels differently, 1,284 in one and 1,800 in another, so say about 1,300 to 1,800 panels.

It was built through a national research program run by MOLIT, working with the city of Seoul and the Nowon-gu district, with companies and universities as partners. So the national government, the city and the district all had a role. In August 2018, Building 102 became the first housing in Korea to earn German Passive House certification. In December 2017, President Moon Jae-in visited, called it Korea's first zero-energy apartment complex, and used it to start a national push to build more like it.

The New York link is Local Law 97. For large apartment buildings over 25,000 sq ft, the yearly carbon limit drops by about half in 2030. The exact figures are 0.00675 t CO₂e per sq ft a year for 2024 to 2029 and about 0.00335 (0.003346640) for 2030 to 2034, a 50.4% cut. About 63% of the buildings LL97 covers are projected to go over their 2030 limits if nothing changes. Your question to the room asks what a NYCHA version of Nowon would look like. To answer it, the class has to think about who pays and who builds, along with the design.

A very well insulated, airtight Passive House envelope cuts how much heating and cooling the apartments need. Heat recovery ventilation, shown on my diagram, is standard in Passive House buildings, but my sources don't list it for Nowon. Then about 1,300 to 1,800 solar panels make most of the power that is left, and the geothermal heat pumps use the ground's steady temperature to heat and cool efficiently.

questions.q: Does NYCHA actually have to meet the LL97 limit you showed?
questions.a: My sources don't say which LL97 limits apply to NYCHA buildings, so I'm not claiming that. What I can say is that the limit for large apartment buildings over 25,000 sq ft drops by about half in 2030. That's why I framed it as a question.

questions.q: Could New York really build something like this? Who would pay for it?
questions.a: Nowon was developed through a national research program run by MOLIT with the city of Seoul and the Nowon-gu district, plus companies and universities. New York would likely need a similar partnership to share the cost and risk of a first project. That's why my NYCHA question points at who pays and who builds, along with the design.

slides.title: Two LEED Gold Buildings
slides.inOneSentence: Amorepacific HQ and Lotte World Tower were both finished in 2017 and both earned LEED Gold, but they got there in very different ways.
background: LEED is a green building rating from the US Green Building Council. It has four levels, Certified, Silver, Gold and Platinum, so Gold is the second highest. Both buildings on this slide were finished in 2017 and both are LEED Gold, which makes them a good pair to compare.

Amorepacific HQ was designed by David Chipperfield Architects, with Arup as the engineers for the building systems. The design won a competition in 2010, construction started in 2014 and the building was finished in 2017. The company has been on this site since 1956. The building is a large cube around a central courtyard, with its proportions worked out so that natural air flow and daylight work well. Three large openings, called hanging gardens, cut through the outside walls and connect the courtyard to the outside, bringing light and air deep inside. Fins on the facade cut sun and glare. It got LEED Gold in 2018 under Core & Shell, which rates the base building only. It has about 22 floors above ground and roughly 7,000 to 8,000 people working there.

Lotte World Tower was designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox (KPF). It is 555 m tall with 123 floors, one of the tallest buildings in the world, and its form draws on Korean ceramics, porcelain and calligraphy. It relies mostly on added systems. It has 720 geothermal wells about 200 m deep, uses Han River water for heating and cooling, and has wind turbines near the top, solar panels and energy recovery wheels that pass heat from outgoing air to incoming air. It also reuses greywater and collects rainwater. One source reports it as the first building over 100 floors to earn LEED Gold.

Amorepacific also won a CIBSE Building Performance Award. CIBSE is the UK professional body for the engineers who design heating, cooling and lighting, and this award is judged on measured performance, meaning real data from the building in use. So Amorepacific has evidence that it works in practice, in addition to its LEED rating.

The main point of the slide is what LEED measures. LEED Gold shows that a building is efficient for its type. The dossier says LEED Gold on Lotte certifies relative efficiency. For energy, LEED compares the design with a basic version of the same building that just meets a basic energy code (general knowledge). So "a basic version of the same tower" in your quote means a computer model of Lotte itself. If someone asks which towers it is compared with, explain that it is a model of the same building and that no other real towers are involved. A 555 m tower still has a huge amount of embodied carbon, which is the carbon released to make all that concrete and steel and to build with it, and it uses a lot of energy for each person inside. So the same LEED Gold rating covers two buildings that reach it in very different ways.

Amorepacific is more like a car that was tested on the road, because its CIBSE award was based on real measured data.

questions.q: What does LEED Gold mean?
questions.a: LEED is the US Green Building Council's green building rating. It has four levels, Certified, Silver, Gold and Platinum, so Gold is the second highest. Buildings earn points for things like energy, water and materials, and the total sets the level.

questions.q: What does Core & Shell mean?
questions.a: It's a LEED rating for the base building: the structure, the outside walls and the central systems like heating and cooling. It leaves out the tenants' interiors. Amorepacific got LEED Gold under Core & Shell in 2018.

questions.q: Why does the CIBSE award matter?
questions.a: CIBSE is the UK professional body for building services engineers, the people who design heating, cooling and lighting. Its Building Performance Award is judged on measured performance, using data from the building in use. So it shows Amorepacific performs well in real life, which adds something a design rating on its own can't show.

questions.q: So which building does more for the climate: Lotte, Amorepacific or Nowon?
questions.a: LEED can't answer that. Its energy points compare each building with a basic version of the same building, and Nowon has no LEED rating at all in my sources, so the three can't be ranked by LEED. Amorepacific has measured data behind its award, and Nowon is a 121-unit apartment complex that aims for net zero. Lotte is efficient for a supertall, but a 555 m tower carries huge embodied carbon and high energy use per person, so I find it hard to argue it does the most for the climate.

questions.q: Lotte has geothermal wells, river water heating and cooling, wind turbines and solar panels. Why criticize it?
questions.a: The equipment helps, but the size of the tower is the bigger issue. Building 555 m and 123 floors takes an enormous amount of concrete and steel, and the carbon from making those materials is released before anyone moves in. LEED Gold shows Lotte is efficient for its type, so it doesn't answer the question of total carbon.

slides.title: Trash Fees and Smart Bins
slides.inOneSentence: How Seoul charges households for trash: priced bags for general trash since 1995, and shared smart bins that weigh food waste and bill each household for it.
background: Since 1995, everyone in Korea, Seoul included, has paid for general trash by buying official priced bags. General trash means anything that is not recycling or food waste, which are kept separate. The more trash you throw out, the more bags you have to buy, so people have a reason to throw out less. This kind of system is called pay as you throw, and Korea's version is the one other countries usually point to.

Food waste goes into shared smart bins instead. A resident taps a household RFID card on the bin, the lid opens, the bin weighs what goes in, and that household is billed for the weight. The 3D diagram on the slide walks through these three steps. The 4.2 kg on the bin's display is only an example.

There is a reward too. A household that cuts its food waste by 10 to 30% compared with the same period a year earlier can earn up to 5,000 points in each evaluation period, worth about ₩5,000. The separated food waste is turned into animal feed, compost and biogas.

The results are on the slide. The bag fees cut trash by about 8% in 1995 and 11% by 1996, both compared with 1994. Seoul Solution warns that the 1995 number may be too high, because many people threw out large items for free that year, so the 1996 number is the more reliable one. For food waste, Korean agency reporting from December 2013 gives a 10 to 30% drop, and a comparison table on the same site gives 9 to 31% for the weighing bins.

New York has made curbside composting mandatory, and buildings can be fined $25 to $100 if they have 1 to 8 units, and $100 to $300 if they have 9 or more. But New York's brown bins don't weigh anything and there is no reward, so a household never learns how much food it throws out. Seoul's bin gives each household its own number every time. That gap becomes the first idea New York could borrow, on slide 19.

questions.q: Doesn't charging for trash make people dump it illegally?

questions.q: Could New York do this?

slides.title: From Landfill to Park
slides.inOneSentence: How Seoul turned Nanjido, its old garbage mountain, into World Cup Park, and how New York is doing the same thing at Freshkills.
background: Nanjido (nahn-jee-doh) was an island in the Han River. Work on an embankment joining it to the mainland began in January 1977, and in 1978 it became Seoul's official dump. It was picked because it was easy to reach and far from downtown.

Over about 15 years the trash piled up into two mounds about 90 m high, roughly as tall as a 30-story building. Korea had no modern system for landfill gas or leachate at the time. Leachate is the dirty liquid that drains out of buried trash. Rotting trash makes methane, and the site gave off methane and toxic gases.

Planning to fix the site started in 1991. In 1993 the city decided to close the dump and stabilize the ground (some sources say dumping ended in 1992). The 3D diagram shows the general idea of the fix: a sealed cap over the trash, wells that collect the gas, and a park on top. The gas is now captured and used. Construction ran from 1996 to 2002, and the site opened as World Cup Park for the 2002 FIFA World Cup. The two mounds became Haneul Park (hah-nool, meaning sky) and Noeul Park (no-ool).

In 2012 the Seoul Energy Dream Center, Korea's first zero-energy public building, opened on the same ground (slide 10). The old trash can't carry a building's weight, so the center stands on piles that reach down to solid ground.

New York is doing the same thing at Freshkills Park on Staten Island. Fresh Kills was once the world's largest landfill, and it is becoming a park of about 2,200 acres that opens in phases. The two cities reached the same answer on their own, on roughly the same timeline, so this slide presents them as equals.

slides.title: The 2026 Landfill Ban
slides.inOneSentence: Since January 1, 2026, Seoul and its region can't bury raw household trash, but they didn't build enough incinerators first, so some trash is now sent to other cities.
background: In 2021, a law banned direct landfilling of household waste in Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi, the area together called the capital region. Direct landfilling means burying raw household trash. Under the ban, trash has to be burned or processed first. The law gave the region a five-year grace period to get ready.

During those five years, local governments mostly did not add incinerator capacity. One news report says they effectively neglected it. Seoul still runs only four public incinerators, in Gangnam, Mapo, Nowon and Yangcheon, and most are 20 to 30 or more years old. The ban still started on schedule on January 1, 2026, with no emergency delay.

From January to June 2026, Seoul's privately handled household waste reached 457 tons a day, a 3.2-fold rise. Public incineration went up by only 80 tons (from 1,921 to 2,001 tons). As a result, much of the trash went to private companies, and some of it left the region. Gangdong district ships waste to private incinerators in Cheonan and Sejong, and Gangnam district plans to send waste to Cheongju. On the map, the straight-line distances from central Seoul are about 85 km to Cheonan, 110 km to Cheongju and 125 km to Sejong. Seoul Economic Daily reported that some trash travels about 130 km, which would be the distance by road.

This is an environmental justice problem, because the trash ends up in communities that didn't make it. Amendments to the Wastes Control Act are pending in the National Assembly with no clear timing, and the nearby city of Seongnam is building a new 500-ton-a-day incinerator to replace an old one.

The slide ends with a question for the class. New York's Local Law 97 fines buildings that go over their emissions limits, and about 63% of covered buildings would miss their 2030 limits if nothing changes. Seoul set its deadline before the incinerators were ready. The question is whether New York's retrofit workers and supply chain can keep up with what LL97 asks for. This is where you stop talking and let the class answer.

slides.title: Restoring Cheonggyecheon
slides.inOneSentence: Seoul removed an elevated highway and uncovered the stream buried under it, and the area gained wildlife, cleaner air and cooler temperatures without the traffic jams people expected.
background: Cheonggyecheon (chung-gyeh-chun) is a stream in central Seoul. It was buried under an elevated highway that carried about 168,000 vehicles a day. From 2003 to 2005, Seoul took the highway down and opened the stream back up. Uncovering a buried stream like this is called daylighting. The project cost about US$281 million and restored about 5.8 km (3.6 miles) of corridor.

Wildlife came back. A Landscape Architecture Foundation case study reports that between 2003 and 2008 plant species went from 62 to 308, insects from 15 to 192, birds from 6 to 36 and fish from 4 to 25. You'll often see a "639% increase in biodiversity" quoted. It's an overall index, so it can't be read as a species count. The counts for each group are safer to give. Plants alone went up about 397%, so there were about five times as many plant species.

The air got cleaner and the area got cooler. Small-particle air pollution fell from 74 to 48 micrograms per cubic meter, about 35% less. The highest cooling estimate says the corridor is 3.3 to 5.9°C cooler than a parallel road 4 to 7 blocks away. Other sources find a smaller effect. WWF says 3 to 4°C cooler than areas 400 m away. Metropolis says the area went from 2.2°C above the Seoul average to 1.3°C above. A peer-reviewed study that pulled many studies together is the most careful source, and it found lower daily average temperatures within about 300 m of the stream.

Many people expected traffic chaos when the highway closed, and it didn't happen. In general, when road space is taken away, some drivers take other routes, some switch to transit, and some trips stop happening. Planners call this reduced demand. It's the opposite of induced demand, where new roads fill up with new traffic. Bus ridership in the corridor rose 15.1% from 2003 to 2008, but Seoul's big 2004 bus reform happened at the same time, so the stream shouldn't get all the credit.

For New York, this is evidence for the debates over the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE), the Cross Bronx Expressway and the Gowanus Expressway. The High Line reused an old rail line, so no drivers lost a road. Cheonggyecheon removed a busy road that drivers used every day, and the gridlock people predicted did not happen.

slides.title: Green Space Close to Home
slides.inOneSentence: Seoul has plenty of park space on average but much less near where people live, so since 2023 it has been adding gardens within a five-minute walk of home, and the slide also covers Seoullo 7017 (2017), rooftop gardens and cool roofs.
background: Seoul counts its park space in two ways. Across the whole city there are 17.74 m² of park per person (2022). If you count only the parks people can reach in a five-minute walk from home, the number drops to 5.65 m² per person, about a third of the average. Both numbers are for Seoul. In 2017 the figures were 16.6 m² citywide and 5.5 m² for neighborhood parks.

That gap is the reason for Garden City Seoul, a plan the city announced in 2023. Its goal is a garden within a five-minute walk of home. The city built 536 municipal gardens in 2024 and set a goal of 1,036 by the end of 2025. Your research didn't find a final count for 2025. The plan has four keywords: emptiness, connection, ecology and sensibility. Seoul also built Seoul Botanic Park in Magok to fill a green-space gap in the southwest. Construction started in November 2015 and it cost ₩215.6 billion.

Seoullo 7017 is a separate, earlier project. It was a road overpass built in 1970. In 2017 it reopened as an elevated walking park, about 1 km long and planted as a living plant library. It cost about US$52 million. The name comes from the two years, 70 for 1970 and 17 for 2017, and the 17 also matches its 17 walkways. New York's High Line is the obvious comparison. The High Line was built on an old elevated rail line, while Seoullo was a road overpass for cars, so Seoul gave road space to people on foot.

The last part of the slide is about roofs. Seoul pays up to 70% of the construction cost of a rooftop garden on a private building, up from 50% before. A study of the Jung-gu district describes the rules as a roof bigger than 99 m², preferably on a building 10 years old or newer. The city says a rooftop garden cuts a building's heating and cooling energy by 12 to 15% on average. The program is small and its totals are reported in scattered pieces, such as 2,227 m² across six new gardens in a 2025 city release. In 2026 the city also started a cool-roof pilot, covering 31,204 m² of roof at 152 sites with heat-reflecting paint for vulnerable households, to cut their summer power bills. The city plans to expand it to whole priority districts.

For New York the useful idea is the way of measuring. Both cities have almost no empty land for new parks, so each new garden or park has to be placed on purpose. If a city counts only park space within walking distance, the neighborhoods with the least nearby green space move to the top of the list.

slides.title: Buses and the Climate Card
slides.inOneSentence: Two Seoul transit moves: the 2004 bus reform, which gave buses their own lanes in the middle of the road and one fare system with the subway, and the 2024 Climate Card, one monthly price for unlimited rides on Seoul metro lines, Seoul buses and Ttareungi bikes.
background: In July 2004 Seoul rebuilt its whole bus network and switched it over in one night. Before the reform, most subway lines shared a fare system, but buses were left out of it. The reform tied them together with one fare based on distance and free transfers between bus and subway. The same fare system later spread to Gyeonggi Province in July 2007 and to Incheon in 2009.

The reform also changed the streets. Main roads got bus lanes in the middle of the road, with island stops where riders wait between the lanes of traffic. Routes were sorted into four colors: blue for long main routes, green for local neighborhood routes, red for express routes to the suburbs and yellow for downtown loops. The four colors made the network easier to read at a glance.

The results were strong, with a few cautions. Bus speeds rose by up to 11 km/h, and travel speeds on main roads rose 33 to 50% (December 2004). Bus accidents fell 24% in the first year. Research linked to UN-Habitat calls this the reform's most dramatic success. Ridership went up too, but the size depends on which years are compared, from about 9 to 21%. UN-Habitat's cautious figure is about 9%, or 406,000 more riders a day (September 2003 to September 2004). UN-Habitat also found that service got much better, but in the first few years the subsidies didn't come down.

The Climate Card came twenty years later. It was announced in September 2023, piloted in January 2024 and fully launched in July 2024. For ₩65,000 a month you get unlimited rides on Seoul metro lines, Seoul-licensed buses including late-night ones, and Ttareungi public bikes. It costs ₩62,000 without bikes, and the youth version is ₩58,000 with bikes. It doesn't cover the Shinbundang Line, buses licensed outside Seoul or metropolitan express buses. Seoul lists River Bus versions at ₩67,000, or ₩70,000 with bikes, but the slide lists the River Bus as planned, so if asked say it is an add-on and is not in the ₩65,000 card. The card has been spreading to nearby cities such as Gimpo, Goyang and Seongnam.

Seoul reports 10 million reloads by April 2025. Each top-up of the pass counts as a reload, so one rider can be counted many times. Seoul hasn't released how many people use the card or how much driving it replaced. New York's closest match is OMNY fare capping. Once you've paid for a set number of rides, the rest of your rides in that period are free. Citi Bike is sold separately. Seoul's version adds bike share and carries a climate name, so the city presents riding transit as part of its climate plan.

slides.explainSimply: The Climate Card works like a gym membership. You pay one flat price for the month, then every extra ride feels free, so you stop asking whether a trip is worth the fare. questions.q: What actually changed in the 2004 bus reform?
questions.a: Seoul switched its whole bus network in one night in July 2004. Main roads got center bus lanes with island stops, and routes were sorted into four colors. Buses also joined the subway in one fare system based on distance, with free transfers.

questions.q: Your slide says ridership rose 9 to 21%. Which is it?
questions.a: It depends on the years compared. Sources give 17.8% for 2004 to 2006, 21.2% for 2004 to 2007 and 9.4% for 2004 to 2017. UN-Habitat's cautious number is about 9%, or 406,000 more daily riders, comparing September 2003 with September 2004. I give the range and never add them together.

questions.q: How many people use the Climate Card, and did it get anyone out of their car?
questions.a: Seoul reports 10 million reloads by April 2025, but each top-up counts as a reload, so one person can be counted many times. The city hasn't released a user count or any data on driving. That missing data is a fair criticism of the program.

questions.q: How is this different from OMNY fare capping in New York?
questions.a: The idea is similar. With OMNY, once you've paid for a set number of rides, the rest of your rides in that period are free. Seoul charges one flat monthly price, includes the Ttareungi bike share and named the pass for the climate. In New York, Citi Bike is a separate membership.

questions.q: Did the bus reform save the city money?
questions.a: Not in the first few years. UN-Habitat found service got much better, but the reform didn't reduce the subsidies the buses needed.

slides.title: Five Ideas for New York
slides.inOneSentence: The five Seoul tools you think New York could borrow, each matched to a gap in New York today, with city retrofit loans as your main recommendation.
background: This slide pulls the whole talk together. Each row pairs a tool Seoul already uses with a gap in New York. Row 02, city loans for building retrofits, is your main recommendation, so it gets the most time.

01 Food waste charged by weight. In Seoul a household taps an RFID card on a shared smart bin. The lid opens, the bin weighs the food waste, and that household is billed for it. Reports show about 9 to 31% less food waste, and households that cut 10 to 30% compared with the year before can earn up to 5,000 points (worth about ₩5,000). New York made curbside composting mandatory, but organics were only 2.4% of residential waste in 2025, up from 1.4% in 2024. Fines were set to start in April 2025, were paused within three weeks and came back on January 1, 2026. The Independent Budget Office (IBO) found that pickup nearly tripled while fines were on and fell about 43% after they stopped. New York's bins give no feedback and no reward. Buildings already have to provide refuse rooms, so a bin that weighs food waste could be written into the building code.

02 City loans for building retrofits. Seoul's Building Retrofit Program (BRP) started in 2008. In 2013 the interest rate dropped from 2.5% to 1.75%, and the loan limit rose from 80% to 100% of the eligible cost. New York's Local Law 97 covers buildings over 25,000 sq ft. It sets a carbon limit for each building and fines owners $268 for every ton of CO₂e over it. About 11% of buildings are over the 2024 to 2029 limits, and about 63% would be over the 2030 limits if nothing changes. The law sets the target and the fine and leaves the money question to owners. A city loan fund on terms like Seoul's, tied to LL97, would give owners a way to pay for the work the law asks for.

03 Balcony solar kits. Seoul's Solar City plan (2017) set a goal of small solar panels on 540,000 apartment balconies, using standard kits renters can install, with published safety and appearance rules. New York has many balconies, fire escapes and railings that produce no power, and your research found no city program for them. The technology is ready. The problems are the code, permits and landlord consent. The three asks are an approved-kit list, a simple Department of Buildings (DOB) permit for a plug-in unit, and a renter's right to install. Germany's balcony solar boom shows the idea can spread once permits are simple.

04 and 05. Idea 04 is a transit pass named for the climate. Seoul's Climate Card costs ₩65,000 a month and includes bike share. New York's OMNY fare capping is similar, but Citi Bike is separate, so the two asks are to put Citi Bike on the same OMNY pass and give it a climate name. Idea 05 is road removal. At Cheonggyecheon, Seoul tore down an elevated highway that carried about 168,000 vehicles a day and opened up the stream buried under it, and the gridlock opponents predicted did not happen. New York has its own live debates about the BQE, a cap over the Cross Bronx Expressway and the Gowanus corridor, and Seoul's traffic record is evidence those debates can use.

slides.title: Three Findings
slides.inOneSentence: The closing slide sums up what worked in Seoul, where Seoul fell short and where New York stands, then gives your one recommendation and opens the discussion.
background: The slide title is plain, and you bring the talk title back out loud. In this talk the carrot means rewards and cheap loans, and the stick means rules and fines. For buildings that already exist, Seoul leaned mostly on carrots and New York leans mostly on the stick. The slide gives three short findings, one line each.

What worked in Seoul. The One Less Nuclear Power Plant program set a goal of saving or producing 2 million TOE of energy, about the output of one nuclear reactor. Seoul reached 2.04 million TOE in June 2014, six months early. Eco-Mileage, a voluntary rewards program for saving energy at home, was the most effective single part. It had 1.68 million participants by June 2014 and saved 190,000 TOE. The retrofit loans at 1.75% are the third example. Eco-Mileage shows that rewards can get very large numbers of people to take part, and the loans gave owners a cheap way to pay for upgrades.

Where Seoul fell short. On January 1, 2026, Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi stopped sending household trash straight to landfills. The ban was passed in 2021 with five years to prepare, but the region didn't build enough incinerators. Seoul runs only four (Gangnam, Mapo, Nowon and Yangcheon), and most are 20 to 30 or more years old. In the first half of 2026, trash handled by private companies rose to 457 tons a day, 3.2 times as much as before, while public incineration grew by only 80 tons. Gangdong district sends trash to private incinerators in Cheonan and Sejong, and Gangnam plans to send some to Cheongju. Some of this trash travels about 130 km by road. The cities receiving it are pushing back.

Where New York stands. LL97 fines owners $268 for each ton of CO₂e over their building's limit, and it leaves the financing to owners. About 63% of covered buildings would be over the 2030 limits if nothing changes. Seoul's landfill ban raises a fair question for New York. Is LL97 asking for retrofits faster than the city's workers and suppliers can deliver them?

Your closing recommendation is the retrofit loans, because LL97 already has the fines and owners still need a way to pay for the work. Then you mention that the full sources are in the submitted PDF and open the floor with your question about Seoul's loans and New York's fines. Backup questions are ready if the room is quiet: Lotte World Tower compared with Nowon EZ House, fines and fairness for low-income families, and park space within walking distance.

questions.q: So which works better, the carrot or the stick?
questions.a: From my research, each one has a weak spot when it's used alone. Seoul's rewards got huge participation, like 1.68 million Eco-Mileage participants, and its loans made upgrades cheap, but its landfill ban came before the incinerators were ready. New York has strong limits and fines, but LL97 doesn't come with city loans like Seoul's. My recommendation is to add Seoul-style loans to the fines New York already has.

questions.q: The landfill ban is a stick. Doesn't Seoul's trash crisis weaken your case for Seoul?
questions.a: It's part of my case. The ban came with five years to prepare, and the region didn't build enough incinerators, so some trash now travels about 130 km by road to other cities. It shows what happens when a rule arrives before the means to follow it. LL97 could run into the same problem if owners don't have the money or the contractors.

questions.q: Did One Less Nuclear Power Plant actually shut down a nuclear plant?
questions.a: The name describes an amount of energy. The goal was 2 million TOE saved or produced, about the output of one reactor, and Seoul reached 2.04 million TOE in June 2014. My research doesn't link it to closing any specific plant.

questions.q: Where is Seoul's trash going now?
questions.a: Seoul's four public incinerators still burn part of it, but their total rose only 80 tons, from 1,921 to 2,001 tons. Trash handled by private companies reached 457 tons a day in the first half of 2026, 3.2 times as much as before. Some districts send it to private incinerators outside the region. Gangdong sends trash to Cheonan and Sejong, and Gangnam plans to send some to Cheongju. Cheongju's operators agreed not to bid on capital-region contracts through the end of next year, as reported in October 2026.

questions.q: Are Seoul's emissions actually going down? What's the latest total?
questions.a: I couldn't find a recent citywide total for Seoul in English sources. I can give you the plan. The 2005 baseline was 52.34 Mt CO₂e, with half of that by 2033 and net zero by 2050. That's why I talk about programs with measured results, like the 2.04 million TOE.

dontSay: Don't give a recent total for Seoul's citywide emissions. It isn't published in English sources you can point to. Use the 2005 baseline of 52.34 Mt and the goal of half by 2033.
Don't call the 1.68 million "households." They are Eco-Mileage participants.
Don't say the trash travels 130 km in a straight line. It's the reported road distance.
Don't say One Less Nuclear Power Plant closed a nuclear reactor.
Don't say LL97 will fail. Say about 63% of buildings are projected to miss the 2030 limits if nothing changes.
Don't call the landfill ban a total failure. It took effect on schedule and is struggling because there aren't enough incinerators.
If Nowon comes up in Q&A, don't use the "100% energy cost" claim. Say up to 61% lower energy costs and about 75 to 80% self-sufficiency.
